content: Leptospirosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. These bacteria are spread through the urine of infected animals. When an infected animal urinates, the bacteria can contaminate water or soil, where they can survive for weeks to months. Humans can become infected by coming into contact with contaminated fresh water, soil, or objects that have been exposed to the urine of infected animals. The most common routes of infection include the bacteria entering the body through the eyes, nose, mouth, or broken skin, such as cuts or scratches. Additionally, consuming food or drinking water that has been contaminated can also lead to infection. Some individuals with leptospirosis may not exhibit any symptoms. However, when symptoms do occur, they can include fever, headache, chills, muscle aches, vomiting, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), red eyes, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and occasionally a rash. Without appropriate treatment using antibiotics, leptospirosis can lead to severe complications, such as damage to the kidneys, liver, or the lining of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis). In some cases, the disease can be fatal. Leptospirosis is found worldwide but is most prevalent in regions with temperate or tropical climates. These areas include South and Southeast Asia, Oceania, the Caribbean, parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Latin America. People are at higher risk of infection if they come into contact with potentially contaminated fresh water, such as lakes and rivers, visit urban areas with poor sanitation, or handle animals or their bodily fluids. Mammals that can carry the infection include rodents, cows, sheep, goats, pigs, horses, dogs, and various wildlife species. Currently, there is no vaccine approved for use in the United States to prevent leptospirosis in humans. Travelers can take several precautions to reduce their risk of infection. These include avoiding contact with fresh water or soil that may be contaminated with animal urine, as well as avoiding contact with objects that could be contaminated, such as animal bedding. It is also important to avoid wading, swimming, or submerging your head in floodwaters or water from lakes, rivers, or swamps, especially after flooding or heavy rain. If avoiding such water is not possible, wearing protective clothing, such as footwear, and covering cuts or wounds with waterproof bandages or dressings is recommended. To further reduce the risk, travelers should ensure that drinking water is safe by boiling it or using appropriate chemical treatments. For some individuals, taking preventive medication before traveling to areas where leptospirosis is common may be an option. It is essential to consult with a healthcare provider before traveling and discuss all planned activities to determine the best preventive measures.
